comment: I want to directly address several aspects of the Little Kate Road multiuse path project in advance of your April 9 presentation at City Council. I appreciate that this is a long email, and I thank you in advance for your patience in reading it. I am writing as a local individual, not as a Holiday Ranch HOA Board member, and am using my local for clarity. As a 20-year homeowner on Holiday Ranch Loop Rd ("HRLR"), I have observed how Little Kate functions for our community. In addition, the multi-use path created on HRLR about 16 years ago in front of my house has given me additional awareness of how the proposed multi-use path plan details for Little Kate will affect the lower Park Meadows neighborhood. I understand that the grant funds have specific qualifying types of work, so I also suggest some alternate uses for the funds that could have greater direct benefits for the safety and well-being of our neighborhood than the Little Kate multi-use path plan. My first concern is that the project's intent, while honorable, does not match the actual situation. The premise is that a re-design of Little Kate, which is along a "Safe Route to School" and aims for designs that support "all ages and abilities", needs a multi-use 12' wide path and roadway narrowing to 11' per direction that is intended to improve safety and comfort for people walking and biking. This change is proposed to be a safety and comfort improvement over the existing layout Little Kate currently has a north-side 4-5' sidewalk, 2 bike lanes (south and north sides), several t-intersections, the PC MARC, and the back of the high school campus. However, the reality is that Little Kate doesn't have substantial problems that would be solved by this project. Many neighborhood attendees at the Feb 24 open discussion voiced their opposition to this project. The constant undertone was that this project is a "solution looking for a problem". First, safety and comfort are worsened on a multi-use path that allows e-bikes. No one has disputed this (ex Round Valley, Rail Trail). On HRLR, speeding e-bikes regularly occupy that multi-use path, forcing pedestrians to jump out of the way, severely increasing safety risks for walkers and slow bicyclists. On both Little Kate and HRLR, bike lanes on both sides of the street, with recently painted clearly visible markings that themselves visually narrow the motorized vehicle lane width, provide ample in-road paths for cyclists going at anything more than strolling speed, which automatically makes existing sidewalk use safer. Second, the most obvious risks to safety for pedestrians and bicyclists along Little Kate (and HRLR) are vehicles - speeding, running through stop signs, failing to yield to non-vehicle users at intersections, driving into opposite lanes of traffic when (illegally) passing vehicles, including buses at bus stops, and excessively fast e-bikes on the HRLR multi-use path. The more-than-10 ft narrowing of the HRLR roadway did not reduce any of the above hazards. It should be noted that Little Kate has a 20-mph speed limit, which seems to never be obeyed, while HRLR has a 25 mph limit, which now has more compliance since a solid double yellow line was recently painted to further narrow the driving lane width visibilities. The project website states what I think is a serious flaw in the team's conclusions that this project is warranted. The basis for the conclusion that Little Kate needs such a drastic reworking for user "safety and comfort" came from flawed data on user counts for the street. The data were collected in one 24-hr count of pedestrians, bicyclists, and drivers on a single day in Sept 2025 (not clear if this was a weekday or a weekend, which have different usages). The impacts of peak vs non-peak use (AM vs late afternoon) and vastly different usage in Sept vs winter or summer were not considered. Most of the time, this roadway is not heavily used - residents living on Little Kate and we who use this street on a daily basis can attest to this. There is a definite "rush hour" each weekday AM and in the late afternoon, and there are seasonal changes in bus vs bike use. Assuming that a single 24 hour period of counts in September can be extrapolated to a 24/7 year-round chronic problem that would mandate major reworking, costs, and many months of disruptions to a prominent neighborhood transportation artery is simply wrong. Another concern I have with the project is that the plan essentially ignores the need for improving accessibility and userfriendliness for the 3 City bus routes in Park Meadows that operate as often as 15 min/bus. The buses encounter one another at several tight stop sign turns in the road, often needing to alternate which bus waits for the other to complete its turn. Narrowing the roadway will not make these maneuvers easier. Have the plan team members confirmed that two City buses can pass each other without side mirrors colliding? Part of the project plan funds allocation is specifically targeted for improved bus stop improvements. There is a great need for this in Park Meadows. However, effort and intent for this are lacking. The plan identifies 2 out of approximately 30 bus stops for "improvements" in 2026, and less than a dozen for 2027. Many of the bus stops are simply poles in the ground in residents' front properties. These get buried in snow up to 3' deep and minimally 4'x4' in area. They are inaccessible to limited-mobility users yearround or people wearing ski boots. Bus users (including students who use the bus to or from school and PCMARC) need to stand and walk in the roadway in order to board or disembark since the buses often remain in the roadway at stops. The plan also proposes ski racks at some bus stops, but that money would be better used for consistent bus stop improvements such as bike racks, ADA accessibility, benches, shelters, etc. City snow removal for the Little Kate project needs to be reassessed. The plan team is aware that existing snow removal along the existing 5' sidewalk has caused significant damage to at least one residential property, ruining landscaping and hitting the house windows. Some driveways are already at lower grade than the existing sidewalk and accumulate so much snow and salt runoff from this snow removal that "ponds" of ice fill the entire sidewalk. The 2.5' "snow storage" along the south side of Little Kate seems inadequate for snow removal from the roadway that will now be closer to the properties on that side of the road, which will impact those properties' landscaping and driveways, as well. This issue needs to be addressed and has not been tagged for budgeting. It is also not clear that City snow removal department budgets are positioned to address the need for better and/or more careful snow removal. Given that the plan requires moving the center of the Little Kate roadway off its current center, it appears that the entire road will need to be torn up and regraded. There is already a drainage problem for snow melt and rain along the north side of Little Kate (see above) - this should be fixed as part of the project, but it is not clear that this has been budgeted for. A major concern for all bus users in Park Meadows is that major road reconstruction will require prolonged construction that will require the entire roadway to be closed for long periods of time. This will severely impact bus access to the entire neighborhood, resulting in more car traffic and associated hazards. These buses are crucially important to Park Meadows residents, High School students, and PC MARC users. Finally, the intent to move forward with the project as it currently stands appears to be to solicit contractor bids in the next month or so. However, in light of concerns of many neighborhood residents, there seems to be a collective desire to continue discussions and dig deeper into the details and specific adjustments before calling the plan finalized and receiving bids for a major project that may have shortcomings that limit its value and outcomes, and precludes better use of the funds for stronger safety and overall benefit. Some suggestions I have for alternative use of the grant funds, still within the parameters of the grant are 1) make every bus stop for the blue and green (and tan) lines between Hotel Thaynes and the Kearns/Monitor intersection ADA-compliant (clearly included in the grant). 2) sharpen the turning angles between Little Kate and intersecting streets (ex: at Holiday Ranch Loop Rd and Little Kate by Stop 20130; both sides of Lucky John - Little Kate intersection) so that vehicles would slow down when making those turns - note that neither of these 2 examples involve bus turns, which need a larger radius) - this would improve pedestrian and bicyclist safety at intersections, which is an important component of Safe Routes to School. 3) signage ahead of bus stops and intersections that are not easily visible due to roadway turns (ex: by Stop 20130) and/or intersections being immediately beyond bus stops (ex: Stops 30800, 30770), and a "blind curve ahead" sign for both the north/eastbound and south/westbound sides of the 90 degree roadway curve at Stop 20130. Such signage serves the Safe Routes to School goal for pedestrians and bicyclists, driver safety, and Bus Stop Improvements since access to the bus stops will be safer. 4) Research possibilities for park-and-ride areas near key bus stops, which would increase accessibility to the bus system, thereby reducing vehicle travel throughout the city, which is an important component of improving pedestrian and bicyclist safety. 5) Consider creating a modest multi-use path on upper Lucky John from Little Kate to American Saddler. This is a fairly wide roadway that has many homes along it, no bus service, no sidewalks, no well-marked bike lanes, and experiences high traffic at high speeds without any safe path for pedestrians and casual bicyclists. As the neighborhood and side streets around this part of Lucky John have many families, it would seem to qualify as part of Safe Routes to School. 6) Hold back some funds for eventual sidewalk and bike lane safety work on Monitor, which was eliminated from an earlier stage of the plan. I implore you to slow down, not rush into bidding on a project that affects so many residents in so many ways, and continue to listen to the community with an open mind to adjust and modify the plans to maximize the end effect, which of course is safety, comfort, and a result that we can all be proud of.
